body:
Why social reform became necessary

During the 19th century, Indian society experienced important movements against caste discrimination and restrictions on women's lives. These movements questioned practices that denied people education, dignity, freedom of choice and equal participation in society.

Two major forms of inequality were especially important: caste-based discrimination and gender-based discrimination. They were closely connected because a woman's opportunities could be restricted both by her gender and by the caste or community to which she belonged.

Caste hierarchy and untouchability

The caste system placed communities within a social hierarchy. Occupations, social status and access to public facilities were often influenced by birth. Communities treated as untouchable faced particularly severe restrictions. In many places, they were prevented from entering temples, using wells maintained for dominant castes, attending schools alongside other children or participating equally in public life.

Untouchability referred to the discriminatory treatment of certain communities as socially or ritually impure. It was not simply a difference in religious belief; it affected everyday activities such as obtaining drinking water, receiving education and moving through public spaces.

These restrictions were not identical throughout India. Their forms and severity varied across regions, communities and periods.

Restrictions on women

Women also faced unequal treatment in education, marriage and property ownership. Child marriage occurred in many communities. Widows could face restrictions on remarriage, dress, participation in ceremonies and control over property. In some regions, the practice of sati involved a widow being burned on her deceased husband's funeral pyre.

These practices must not be treated as universal features of every Indian community. Reform movements developed in response to particular social conditions and differed according to region, religion and caste.

How reform movements developed

Schools, newspapers, pamphlets and books helped people discuss social customs and spread criticism of inequality. Reformers used different methods: some interpreted religious texts to challenge harmful customs, others established schools and associations, and still others demanded changes in laws.

Increasingly, people belonging to oppressed communities organized movements themselves. Rather than depending entirely on others to speak for them, they demanded recognition, access to public facilities and a voice in political decisions.

Social reform means organized efforts to change practices or institutions considered unjust. Anti-caste assertion specifically emphasizes the dignity, equality and rights claimed by communities facing caste discrimination.

Two related directions of change

  • Reform of social practices: Campaigns against sati and child marriage, support for widow remarriage, and efforts to improve women's education and property rights.
  • Assertion of equal rights: Movements against untouchability and caste hierarchy, demands for access to public water and temples, community organization and political representation.

Education linked the two directions. It could help women become economically independent and help excluded communities challenge restrictions on occupations and public participation.

A law could remove a legal restriction without immediately ending social opposition. For example, permitting widow remarriage did not mean that remarried widows were readily accepted by all families and communities.

Prelims focus

  • Caste discrimination could restrict access to education, public water sources and temples.
  • Women's reform addressed marriage, widowhood, education and property rights.
  • Printed books, newspapers and pamphlets helped spread reform ideas during the 19th century.
  • Anti-caste movements increasingly involved organization and leadership from oppressed communities themselves.
  • Trap: Legal reform and actual social acceptance are not the same thing.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, 2020–21, Chapter 8, Women, Caste and Reform, printed pp. 94–96 and 99–102.]

pictures.caption: Education became an important means of challenging social restrictions in 19th-century India.

pictures.alt: Social reform challenged restrictive practices, anti-caste assertion demanded equal rights, and education linked both.
pictures.caption: Social reform and anti-caste assertion addressed connected but distinct forms of inequality.

title: Social Inequality and the Rise of Reform in Colonial India

body:
Jyotirao Phule and the challenge to caste hierarchy

Jyotirao Govindrao Phule (1827–1890) was an important social reformer from Maharashtra. He criticized the idea that a person's social position and opportunities should be determined by birth. His work was especially associated with the interests of Shudras and Ati-Shudras, terms used in his historical social and political arguments.

Phule opposed claims of hereditary superiority made by dominant castes. He also argued that social change would remain incomplete if oppressed communities continued to be excluded from education and public life.

His criticism extended beyond caste alone. He addressed the problems faced by women, labourers and other disadvantaged sections of society.

Girls' education and Savitribai Phule

Jyotirao and Savitribai Phule worked to promote girls' education in Pune. In 1848, they opened a school for girls there. Savitribai became a pioneering woman teacher and reformer.

Women's education was socially controversial because some people believed that girls should remain within the household and that schooling would weaken established family customs. The Phules challenged these assumptions by treating education as a means of developing confidence and independence.

For the Phules, the struggle against caste inequality and the struggle for women's education were connected. Denying education helped preserve unequal social relationships; extending it could provide people with the knowledge needed to question those relationships.

Satyashodhak Samaj, 1873

Jyotirao Phule founded the Satyashodhak Samaj, or Truth-Seeking Society, in 1873 in Maharashtra.

The association sought to challenge caste discrimination and the authority that hereditary caste status exercised over social and religious life. It emphasized equality and encouraged people from oppressed communities to develop self-respect and organize for their own advancement.

The significance of the society lay not merely in criticizing inequality but in providing an organization through which people could act collectively.

Satyashodhak Samaj: Jyotirao Phule, Maharashtra, 1873. Its central concern was opposition to caste-based inequality and the promotion of social equality.

Gulamgiri and the language of slavery

In 1873, Phule published Gulamgiri, meaning Slavery. He compared the oppression of lower castes in India with slavery in America and dedicated the work to those who had struggled against slavery in the United States.

This comparison expressed Phule's argument that social domination was not justified simply because it had existed for a long time. He also offered his own historical interpretation of how caste domination had developed. That interpretation should be understood as part of his critique of caste, rather than as an established historical fact about ancient population movements.

Why Phule's approach was distinctive

  • He connected caste equality with education.
  • He gave special importance to the dignity and advancement of Shudras and Ati-Shudras.
  • He worked alongside Savitribai Phule to challenge restrictions on women's education.
  • He founded an organization rather than limiting his efforts to individual writings.
  • He compared caste oppression with slavery to explain the injustice of inherited social subordination.

Prelims focus

  • 1827: Birth of Jyotirao Phule.
  • 1848: Jyotirao and Savitribai Phule opened a school for girls in Pune.
  • 1873: Formation of the Satyashodhak Samaj.
  • 1873: Publication of Gulamgiri.
  • Gulamgiri: Connected criticism of caste oppression with the struggle against American slavery.
  • Trap: Satyashodhak Samaj was founded by Jyotirao Phule, not by Narayana Guru or Periyar.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, 2020–21, Chapter 8, Women, Caste and Reform, printed pp. 98 and 103–104; Press Information Bureau, President of India's address to the 95th All India Marathi Literary Conference, 24 April 2022, paragraphs on the Phule reform tradition, consulted 20 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: The two major dates associated with Jyotirao Phule's educational and organizational work.

title: Jyotirao and Savitribai Phule: Education, Satyashodhak Samaj and Gulamgiri

body:
Social conditions in Kerala

Sree Narayana Guru (1856–1928) was a major social and spiritual reformer of Kerala. He came from the Ezhava community, which faced caste-based restrictions in traditional Kerala society.

Restrictions affected religious worship, public life, employment and education. Some communities were excluded from temples or denied equal opportunities because of their caste identity.

Narayana Guru argued that such distinctions were inconsistent with the essential equality of human beings. He challenged caste hierarchy while using spiritual teaching and community organization as important means of reform.

Aruvippuram consecration, 1888

In 1888, Narayana Guru consecrated a Shiva image at Aruvippuram in present-day Kerala. The event was important because prevailing caste conventions reserved many priestly functions and religious privileges for particular castes.

By performing the consecration, Guru challenged the view that religious authority depended upon hereditary caste status.

This event should be distinguished from a campaign for admission into an already existing temple. Its immediate significance lay in asserting the right of a person outside the traditionally privileged priestly castes to perform a religious consecration.

His message of human equality

Narayana Guru's best-known message expressed the ideal of one caste, one religion and one God for humankind.

The message opposed discrimination based on caste and emphasized common human dignity. It did not mean that all existing religions had been administratively merged into a single religious institution. It was an ethical and spiritual declaration of unity.

Education was equally important in Guru's programme. He believed that knowledge, improved social practices and collective effort could help marginalized communities overcome exclusion.

Sree Narayana Dharma Paripalana Yogam, 1903

The Sree Narayana Dharma Paripalana Yogam (SNDP Yogam) was established in 1903 to promote the advancement of disadvantaged communities, particularly Ezhavas.

Dr. Palpu played an important role in organizing the association. Narayana Guru became its first president, while the poet and reformer Kumaran Asan served as its first secretary.

The organization encouraged education, social improvement, economic advancement and religious participation. It showed how a spiritual reform movement could develop an institutional form.

1888 identifies the Aruvippuram consecration; 1903 identifies the SNDP Yogam. These are different events with different immediate purposes.

Connection with temple-access struggles

The wider movement against untouchability in Kerala also included struggles over access to public roads near temples. The Vaikom Satyagraha (1924–1925) challenged restrictions on the use of roads surrounding the Vaikom temple in Travancore.

It is important to identify its immediate demand correctly: access to the roads around the temple, rather than unrestricted entry into the temple's interior. Narayana Guru's followers and the SNDP tradition were associated with this broader struggle.

Prelims focus

  • Sree Narayana Guru: Kerala; Ezhava community; opposition to caste discrimination.
  • 1888: Aruvippuram Shiva consecration.
  • 1903: Establishment of SNDP Yogam.
  • SNDP Yogam: Narayana Guru, first president; Kumaran Asan, first secretary; Dr. Palpu, major organizer.
  • Vaikom Satyagraha, 1924–1925: Campaign for access to roads around the Vaikom temple.
  • Trap: SNDP Yogam was established in 1903, not in 1873.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, 2020–21, Chapter 8, printed p. 102; Kerala Tourism, Sree Narayana Guru, Aruvippuram Siva Temple, section on the 1888 consecration, consulted 20 November 2026; Kerala Tourism, Formation of SNDP Yogam, section on the association's formation and officers, consulted 20 November 2026; Kerala Tourism, Vaikom Satyagraha, section on the movement's objectives and chronology, consulted 20 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: From a challenge to caste restrictions in worship to an organization for wider social uplift.

title: Narayana Guru: Spiritual Equality and Organized Social Uplift in Kerala

body:
Periyar and the demand for dignity

E.V. Ramasamy Naicker (1879–1973), widely known as Periyar, was a prominent social reformer associated with the Tamil region of southern India.

He strongly criticized caste hierarchy, hereditary social privilege and the unequal treatment of women. He argued that people could not attain genuine freedom while remaining subject to humiliating social distinctions.

Periyar had been associated with the Indian National Congress but became increasingly critical of caste inequalities that persisted within public and political life. For him, political independence alone could not ensure equality unless discriminatory social practices were also challenged.

The Self-Respect Movement, 1925

Periyar launched the Self-Respect Movement in 1925. Its central aim was to remove the sense of inferiority imposed on people through caste hierarchy and to promote social equality and individual dignity.

The movement emphasized rationalism, meaning the use of reason and critical examination rather than unquestioning acceptance of authority. Periyar criticized religious practices and interpretations that, in his view, supported caste superiority and male domination.

He also emphasized non-Brahmin assertion and questioned the concentration of social authority in hereditary priestly institutions.

Self-respect in this movement meant that a person should not regard themselves as inferior because of caste, birth or gender. Social dignity was treated as a right, not a privilege granted by another group.

Women and the reform of marriage customs

Periyar regarded women's freedom as essential to social reform. He opposed child marriage, enforced restrictions on widows and customs that denied women an equal position within marriage.

The movement promoted Self-Respect marriages, which rejected the necessity of Brahmin priests and elaborate religious rituals. Such ceremonies emphasized the agreement of the couple and commonly used their own language rather than Sanskrit ritual formulas.

Self-Respect marriages became an important expression of the movement's opposition to caste-based priestly authority. The movement also supported inter-caste marriages and greater freedom of choice for women.

Periyar and Vaikom

Periyar participated in the Vaikom Satyagraha of 1924–1925 in Travancore. The struggle sought to end caste-based restrictions on movement along roads surrounding the Vaikom temple.

The campaign preceded the formal beginning of Periyar's Self-Respect Movement in 1925. It should not be described as a movement founded solely by Periyar.

How Periyar's approach differed

Narayana Guru challenged caste hierarchy partly by asserting equal spiritual and religious rights. Periyar placed stronger emphasis on rationalist criticism of religiously justified hierarchy and on changing everyday social customs, especially marriage practices.

Both opposed caste humiliation, but their methods and emphasis were not identical.

Prelims focus

  • Periyar: E.V. Ramasamy Naicker; associated with the Tamil region.
  • 1925: Beginning of the Self-Respect Movement.
  • Central ideas: Social dignity, rationalism, opposition to caste hierarchy and women's equality.
  • Self-Respect marriages: Challenged the compulsory role of hereditary priests and elaborate religious rituals.
  • 1924–1925: Periyar participated in the Vaikom Satyagraha.
  • Trap: Participation in Vaikom does not mean that Periyar founded the Vaikom movement.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, 2020–21, Chapter 8, printed pp. 104–105; Tamil Nadu History Congress, The Self-Respect Movement of Periyar, proceedings of the Chidambaram session, sections on the movement and Self-Respect marriages, consulted 20 November 2026; Kerala Tourism, Vaikom Satyagraha, section on participants and objectives, consulted 20 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: A simple marriage ceremony became a visible expression of equality and freedom of choice.
